Official minutes of the Troy, Michigan Board of Education regular meeting held March 18, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Dr. Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present were board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler; Superintendent Machesky; and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Zawislak, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 125 members of the audience attended.

Recognitions opened the meeting. Assistant Superintendent Christine DiPilato announced that 28 Troy School District student musicians were selected for the 2025 Michigan All-State Bands and Orchestras, having rehearsed and performed in Grand Rapids from January 23-25 during the annual Michigan Music Conference; Boulan Park instrumental music teacher Joe Havrilla was invited to speak, and certificates were presented to 14 high school and 14 middle school students. A TSD Mission Moment recognized Larson Middle School eighth grader Sanvi Mandvekar, who won the 2025 Oakland County Spelling Bee in the ninth round (spelling 'ordanance') over more than 80 competitors and will advance to the 2025 Scripps National Spelling Bee in Washington, D.C. in May; Brian Zawislak introduced her. The Student Spotlight featured TSD Creative Guild members Vannessa Luu and Gabrielle Robinson, recognized for a kindness-focused podcast, introduced by Creative Content Producer Thomas Butcher.

There were no additions or deletions and no public communication on agenda items. On a motion by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, the board approved consent agenda items A through E by a 7-0 vote: minutes of the February 11, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the February 25, 2025 Board Meeting; the January 2025 Treasurer's Report; Budget Amendment #2; and rescheduling the April 15, 2025 board meeting to April 22, 2025.

Under Business, three actions each passed 7-0. On a motion by Dr. Melton, supported by Mr. Haupt, the bid for site work and signage (Smith) was awarded as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. On a motion by Mrs. Potts, supported by Mrs. Anne, the bid for interior painting services was awarded to RNC Paint Systems in the amount of $50,000.00 as an expenditure of the General Operating Fund. On a motion by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Alic, a furniture purchase for Barnard, Bemis, Hill, Martell, Morse, Troy Union and select areas at Troy High School was approved for an amount not to exceed $5,286,379.00 through pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums), as outlined in a TMP memo dated February 28, 2025.

The extracted text ends mid-sentence within the furniture resolution, so any subsequent student representative reports, non-agenda public communication, board member comments, and adjournment are not captured. What it is: Secondary Math Updates presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education, dated May 6, 2025.

Vision: Drawing on NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics - all students as "doers of mathematics" developing deep understanding.
Professional learning: 2024 Math Summer Institute; back-to-school PD days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math (IM) and NWEA; monthly job-embedded PD for Honors Algebra 1; October/January/March district PD days; a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach, and intervene.
Family support: IM "Family Support Materials," lesson summaries, and a Family Math Night for Math 7 families.

Honors Algebra 1 enrollment (2021-22 -> 2024-25):
- Grade 7: 2% -> 1% -> 1% -> 8%
- Grade 8: 36% -> 37% -> 35% -> 50%

NWEA MAP Growth: Computer-adaptive, nationally normed assessment (used by 16M+ students); reports RIT (Rasch Unit) scores, growth over time, projected growth, and disaggregated data. In 2024-25, grades 6-8 and Algebra 1 tested Fall and Spring (Math 7 also Winter). In 2025-26, grades 6-8 and all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will test Fall, Winter, and Spring.
Next steps: use as a screener; build cohort data; Fall-to-Spring comparison; Summer 2025 Data Retreat with administrators; continued PD in 2025-26.

Student perception (1,932 responses): 93% call class welcoming; 90% agree "I know I can be good at math"; 88% value trying over being right first; 79% feel prepared for the next level; 59% say lessons are "just right." Challenges: 45% do not enjoy math; 34% want more specific feedback.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Secondary Math Updates presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its May 6, 2025 workshop, reviewing the district's middle and high school mathematics program, professional learning, assessment strategy, and student feedback.

The stated vision frames all students as "doers of mathematics," citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, with goals that students develop deep mathematical understanding, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience its wonder, joy, and beauty. Implementation is supported through professional learning: a 2024 Math Summer Institute; back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math (IM) and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; full days of district learning in October, January, and March; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and provide intervention for struggling students.

Family support is provided through IM "Family Support Materials" that describe big ideas in plain language, IM lesson summaries written in student-friendly language (useful for absent students and for families), and a Family Math Night for families of Math 7 students.

The presentation reports Honors Algebra 1 enrollment trends by grade across 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25. Grade 7 enrollment was 2%, then 1%, 1%, and 8%; Grade 8 enrollment was 36%, 37%, 35%, and 50% - a marked jump in both grades in 2024-25. Cohorts are identified as current 9th graders (Class of 2028), current 8th graders (Class of 2029), and current 7th graders (Class of 2030).

On assessment, the district uses NWEA MAP Growth (Measures of Academic Progress), a computer-adaptive, nationally normed, standards-aligned assessment used by over 16 million K-12 students. In 2024-25 all students in grades 6-8 and those enrolled in Algebra 1 took MAP Growth in Fall and Spring, with Math 7 students also testing in Winter to inform placement into Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1. In 2025-26 all grades 6-8 and all students in Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will test in Fall, Winter, and Spring. MAP Growth provides RIT (Rasch Unit) scores indicating instructional level, growth over time, projected growth based on national norms, and data disaggregated by subgroup. Slides reference Fall 2024-25 achievement data. Next steps include using MAP as a screener to identify students needing intervention or extension, building cohort data to track grade-level growth, comparing Fall to Spring (spring testing underway), using district data with teachers in late summer, holding a Summer 2025 Data Retreat with administrators, and continuing professional learning in 2025-26.

Student perception data from 1,932 respondents is summarized. Celebrations: 93% said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had many opportunities to interact; 88% agreed it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed "I know I can be good at math"; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges: 34% would like more specific feedback on how to improve their work, and 45% do not enjoy learning math (a further challenge figure is truncated in the extracted text).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A May 6, 2025 workshop presentation summarizing community feedback from Troy School District's Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) process, which aims to right-size the four middle schools, resolve "double splits," and avoid high-school impact. After five community listening sessions and surveys, an adult survey drew 1,777 responses (70.1% favoring some version of "Option C") and a student survey drew 1,229. The deck compares a No-Change scenario against Option C boundary maps and projected 2027 middle-school enrollments, with the Board set to make a determination in May.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: "Attendance Area Review Community Feedback" presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (May 6, 2025), reporting results of the AARC engagement phase.

Process phases: (1) Discovery - committee research/recommendations; (2) Recommendation (January) - options to the board; (3) Feedback (March-April) - four listening sessions (one per middle school) plus a community survey; (4) Determination (May) - board decides.
AARC goals: right-size middle schools/equal student ratios; resolve double splits; no impact on high schools.

Engagement results:
- 5 community meetings (2 at Larson due to Spring Break).
- Feedback form: 31 responses, 74% from Troy Union.
- Adult survey: 1,777 responses; 90.7% parent/guardian of a current student; most-attended schools Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), Hamilton (240); 53 live in Somerset Apartments; 60.8% familiar with AARC; 70.1% favor some version of Option C.
- Student survey: 1,229 responses; top schools Baker (344), Boulan Park (309), IA East (284), Larson (216); of 547 who split after 5th grade, 70% felt neutral; of 300 who split after 8th grade, 88% felt neutral.

Enrollment scenarios (middle schools):
- No Change: 4 middle schools; 2,940 pupils (Dec 2024) -> ~2,526 by 2027. 2027 boundary: Baker 517, Boulan 793, Larson 750, Smith 466.
- Option C: Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682; all Troy Union to Smith; Somerset Apartments (319 students) to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools.
- Option C - Only TU (updated after 1/14/25 workshop): Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, Smith 591.
Next steps: Board consideration and decision in May.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An "Attendance Area Review Community Feedback" slide deck presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at the May 6, 2025 workshop, reporting on the community-engagement results of the district's Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) process. The AARC work is organized into four phases: Phase 1 Discovery (committee formed; research, analysis, and planning; developing potential recommendations); Phase 2 Recommendation in January (committee gives the board options and the board decides whether to proceed); Phase 3 Feedback in March-April (four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, plus a community survey); and Phase 4 Determination in May (staff summarize feedback and the board determines any changes). The committee's three goals are to right-size the middle schools with equal student ratios (Goal 1), resolve "double splits" (Goal 2), and have no impact on the high schools (Goal 3).

Engagement figures: the district held five community meetings (two at Larson Middle School because of Spring Break). Recurring questions included the preferred time to split students (elementary-to-middle vs. middle-to-high), whether high-school boundaries should move, whether middle-school splits could be reduced another way, how to handle Somerset Apartments (which feed six schools), how long "legacy" status would continue for a family, mental-health and social/emotional impacts of a middle-to-high split under Option C, and whether open enrollment could be offered at Larson, Smith, and others.

Survey results: the feedback form drew 31 responses, 74% from Troy Union families, with open-ended themes including Troy Union to Larson (6), to Troy High (3), to Smith (3), "consider other options" (8), mental-health impacts (5), moving high-school boundaries (3), removing all splits (3), and no middle-to-high splits (5). The adult survey drew 1,777 responses, 90.7% from a parent/guardian of a current student; the highest counts of respondents' students attend(ed) Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), and Hamilton (240), with 53 living in Somerset Apartments. About 60.8% were familiar with the AARC process (most having read about it on the website or in the weekly newsletter), and 70.1% favored some version of Option C. The student survey (optional for middle and high school students) drew 1,229 responses, top schools being Baker (344), Boulan Park (309), IA East (284), and Larson (216); of 547 students who experienced a split after 5th grade, 70% felt neutral, and of 300 who experienced a split after 8th grade, 88% felt neutral.

Enrollment scenarios: Under "No Change," all Somerset Apartment students attend Boulan Park; the four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024, projected to fall to 2,526 by 2027 (a reduction of 400+). The 2024 boundary counts were Baker 631, Boulan 847, Larson 863, and Smith 599; maintaining the existing boundary yields 2027 counts of Baker 517, Boulan 793, Larson 750, and Smith 466. Under "Option C," projected counts are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, and Smith 682, with all Troy Union students going to Smith, students in community housing following their assigned elementary to its middle school, and Somerset Apartments' 319 students going to Boulan Park from six elementary schools. A refined "Option C - Only TU," updated after the January 14, 2025 board workshop, projects Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, and Smith 591, with Troy Union students split (illustrated as roughly 80 to Smith and 125 to Larson from a fall 2027 cohort of about 205). Next steps: Board of Education consideration and decision in May.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education workshop on May 6, 2025, this slide deck compiles community feedback gathered during the Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) process, which is evaluating middle-school attendance boundary changes for implementation in fall 2027.

Process and goals. The review runs in four phases: Phase 1 Discovery (committee formation, research, potential recommendations); Phase 2 Recommendation in January (committee presents options to the Board); Phase 3 Feedback in March-April (listening sessions plus a community survey); and Phase 4 Determination in May (staff summarize feedback and the Board decides). The committee's three goals are to right-size the middle schools with more equal student ratios, resolve 'double splits,' and avoid any impact on the high schools. Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school with a second at Larson because of spring break.

Meeting feedback themes included the preferred time to split students (elementary-to-middle versus middle-to-high), whether high school boundaries could move, alternative handling of Somerset Apartments (currently feeding six schools), the duration of legacy/grandfathering for families, mental-health and social-emotional impacts of a middle-to-high split under Option C, and possible open enrollment for Larson, Smith, and others.

Survey results. The open-ended feedback form drew 31 responses, 74% from Troy Union families. The adult survey drew 1,777 responses: 90.7% were parents/guardians of current students, 53 lived in Somerset Apartments, and 60.8% were familiar with the AARC process. The largest respondent groups' students attend Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), and Hamilton (240). 70.1% favored some version of Option C (31.8% specifically preferred Option C), and 76.1% had no opinion or did not want the Board to consider any other option. Importance ratings ran high for the travel distance students face (81.3%), balancing enrollment (80.7%), not changing high school boundaries (76.5%), limiting families impacted (76%), and eliminating double splits (73%). The student survey drew 1,229 responses (highest from Baker 344, Boulan Park 309, IA East 284, Larson 216); 547 students had experienced a split after 5th grade (70% neutral) and 300 after 8th grade (88% neutral).

Enrollment outcomes. Under 'No Change,' the four middle schools fall from 2,940 pupils (December 2024) to 2,526 by 2027, projected as Baker 517, Boulan 793, Larson 750, and Smith 466, with all Somerset Apartments students attending Boulan Park. Under 'Option C,' projections are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, and Smith 682: all Troy Union students would attend Smith, students in community housing would follow their assigned elementary to that school's middle school, and Somerset Apartments' 319 students (drawn from six elementaries) would attend Boulan Park. A 'TU only' variant of Option C (updated after the January 14, 2025 Board workshop) yields Baker 517, Boulan 793, Larson 625, and Smith 591. The Somerset Apartments elementary breakdown totals 319 students: Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, and Morse 47, all routed to Boulan Park Middle School. Next steps are Board consideration and a decision in May 2025.

Forwarded to the Troy School District Board of Education, this staff memo tabulates Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) survey results at successive points in the feedback window, allowing comparison as response counts grew.

Adult survey, April 24 snapshot. At 1,221 responses, 88% were current parents/guardians and 32 respondents were from Somerset Apartments. Most were aware of the process, and over 90% had read about it on the website or in weekly updates. A majority preferred Option C when asked, while a majority also had no opinion or did not want the Board to consider other options. Importance ratings were: eliminating double splits 75%; eliminating all splits even if more families are disrupted 53%; balancing enrollment 83%; limiting families impacted 80%; travel distance 80%; not impacting high school boundaries 75%; and a split occurring from elementary to middle school 73%. On mechanisms, 51% would support or had no preference on offering additional SOC to limit changes, 65% would rather the district increase SOC (or had no preference) than close a middle school, and 63% wanted Open Enrollment offered as a balancing method.

Adult survey, April 29 snapshot. With responses risen to 1,777, 90.7% were current parents/guardians and 53 were from Somerset Apartments. 60.8% were aware of the process and 92.9% had read about it online or in updates. 70.1% now favored some version of Option C (with 11% having attended Troy Union), 31.8% specifically preferred Option C, and 76.1% had no opinion or did not want other options considered. Updated importance ratings were: double splits 73%; all splits 52.3%; balancing enrollment 80.7%; limiting families impacted 76%; travel distance 81.3%; no high school impact 76.5%; and elementary-to-middle split 72.7%. On mechanisms, 67.2% supported or had no preference on additional SOC, 66.3% preferred increasing SOC over closing a middle school, and 63.2% wanted Open Enrollment.

Student survey, April 28 snapshot. Of 1,229 responses, 44.5% had experienced a split after 5th grade (547 students, 70% of whom felt neutral about it) and 24.4% had experienced a split after 8th grade (300 students, 88% neutral). 54.4% identified elementary-to-secondary as the best time for a split. 63.5% considered eliminating the double split important, while 54.1% did not know or did not consider eliminating all splits important (46% did). Additional ratings included: distributing students evenly among middle schools 61.2%; limiting the number of students facing a change 70.5%; travel distance/time 82.2%; and keeping the Athens and Troy High attendance areas as they are 53.2%. All collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on May 6, 2025, this slide deck documents the district's K-5 writing curriculum review and its resulting materials recommendation. The review is grounded in Michigan's K-5 Writing Standards, quoted at length, which frame writing as a way of offering and supporting opinions, demonstrating understanding of subjects studied, and conveying real and imagined experiences to external audiences.

Team and process. The work was led by an elementary Literacy Leadership Team assembled to represent every grade level, building, and department. Its membership included 12 elementary principals, 7 literacy specialists, 6 ELD specialists, 3 media specialists, 8 special education representatives, 8 Teaching & Learning members, and roughly a dozen teachers at each grade from kindergarten through fifth. The team studied student writing samples across grade levels and years and reviewed academic, demographic, process, and perception data. A Writing Pathways formative assessment was administered in April 2025, writing rubrics were analyzed, and a parent survey was conducted. The deck cites John Hattie (2023) on holding high expectations for all students, avoiding labels such as 'bright' or 'struggler,' being clear about learning goals, and teacher collaboration.

Findings. Areas of success included explicit and responsive instruction, student voice and choice, reflections of identity, critical thinking, the volume and scope of writing, coverage of state writing standards, and real-world connections and application. Areas of growth included explicit teaching of grammar and spelling, support for handwriting and typing, interdepartmental learning with special education and ELD, and family engagement around writing instruction and support at home. The team engaged in shared learning tied to the district strategic plan, reviewed the Michigan Writing Standards, and consulted outside sources including a What Works Clearinghouse/IES practice guide on teaching elementary students to be effective writers, Steve Graham on creating a classroom vision for teaching writing, the National Writing Project's 'Writing for Life,' and a Zaner-Bloser review on why writing workshops work.

Program review. The team purposely reviewed K-5 programs offering year-long writing curricula. Teacher preference strongly favored Writing Units of Study at 90%, followed by Benchmark Education Writing Workshop at 6%, Being a Writer at 4%, and Step Up to Writing and Writing By Design at 0% each.

Early adopters and recommendation. A cohort of 24 classroom teachers, representing every grade level and every school, piloted updated units; 100% reported that the updates were helpful to their instruction and had an impact on student learning, and said identified needs - grammar, spelling, tools for ensuring access for all, and family engagement and celebration - had been addressed. Family and staff engagement included a family survey, principal presentations of the review process at PTO meetings, an open family night, and job-embedded professional learning at which K-5 teachers were informed and could give feedback. The recommendation is to adopt Writing Units of Study (2024, 2025), supported by professional learning in both summer and back-to-school sessions, ongoing job-embedded learning to ensure rigor, continued development of student digital writing portfolios, and parent engagement through family letters and community learning nights.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Submitted in May 2025 by Natalie Haezebrouck and Lisa McDonald, this narrative accompanies the Troy School District's elementary writing materials adoption and lays out the rationale and the multi-year literacy work behind it.

Rationale. The district states that it regularly reviews its curricular materials and has updated its philosophy of curricular review to take a comprehensive look at programming as a whole - understanding instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data - rather than simply seeking new materials. It emphasizes a sustained commitment to a high-quality writing curriculum aligned with Michigan's writing standards. While CORE ELA programs have supported the five pillars of literacy (phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension), those programs have historically offered limited support for writing instruction; to address that gap and ensure full rigor with state standards, Troy has consistently implemented an additional writing curriculum alongside whatever reading program it has used. The district views writing instruction as equally critical to student success as reading and, being in its review cycle, is evaluating comprehensive writing programs that function independently of any reading curriculum. The last writing adoption was in 2016.

Comprehensive literacy system. The memo describes the elementary comprehensive literacy system built since the prior adoption, organized around several components. A strong leadership team represents all grade levels, buildings, and departments, meeting regularly for shared learning, data review, and goal-setting. A vital professional learning community was strengthened through structural changes: using common prep time, opportunities for teachers to observe grade-level peers, vertical observations, district job-embedded lab days for each grade level to learn together in classrooms with students, principal and Teaching & Learning collaborative walk-throughs, administrators positioning themselves as co-learners, continuous support from building literacy specialists, and learning partnerships with universities. High-quality classroom instruction is supported by professional learning communities and on-site support, close observation and monitoring of student progress, and immediate, effective intervention when students are not progressing; expanded professional learning includes new-teacher onboarding in literacy, assessment, and MTSS, district PD on handwriting, phonics, and upper-grade word work/spelling, vertical alignment and resource development around writing genres, Summer Homegrown Institutes, and small-group intervention training emphasizing writing support.

The memo also outlines a system for assessing and monitoring programs - rooted in teachers' close observation of students' literacy behaviors with formative and summative progress monitoring (citing Afflerbach, 2007) - and effective, timely literacy intervention that prioritizes early identification and early intervention within the district's MTSS, supported by high-quality ongoing learning and fidelity of implementation supplementary to Tier One instruction. The extracted text is truncated before any specific materials recommendation, cost, or vote details.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared for member-district consideration ahead of the 2025 bylaws vote, this 'amendments at a glance' document from the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) lists the proposed changes to its bylaws and sorts them into non-substantive corrections and substantive content revisions, giving a rationale for each.

Clerical and grammatical revisions. Four changes are described as clerical or grammatical and as not changing the meaning of the bylaws. In Article V, Section 3 (Place of Meeting), the truncated word 'off' is corrected to 'office.' In Article VIII, Section 2 (Term of Office), the stray first word 'Ther' is corrected to 'The.' In Article IX, Section 4 (The Government Relations Committee), the word 'on' is added after 'information' for clarity; the section confirms the Government Relations Committee is a standing committee whose purpose is to receive information on legislative matters to share with member districts and advocate for public education, and that it meets at least six times per year. In Article XIV, Section 2 (Dealing with the Association), a duplicated phrase is removed from the provision addressing contracts or transactions between the Association and its directors or officers.

Content revisions. Several sections were revised for content. Article VII, Section 4 (Notice) is amended to delete language referring to sending meeting notices via U.S. mail and fax, described as outdated modes of communication; as revised, notice of any special meeting of the Board of Directors is given at least two days in advance by written notice delivered personally or by phone, fax, or email to each director's contact information as shown in the Association's records, or five days' notice by mail, with a director's attendance constituting waiver of notice except when the director attends solely to object to an unlawfully called meeting. A new Article VII, Section 10 (Board Operating Procedures) is added, requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used in conjunction with the bylaws; the rationale notes the Board recently adopted such procedures, which further define roles, responsibilities, and timelines. Article VIII, Section 6 (The Secretary) is revised so that, at the discretion of the Board of Directors on an annual basis, the office of Secretary may be divided into two roles - Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary; the rationale explains that with a board of seven to nine directors it is helpful to split the role and provide additional leadership opportunities. The Secretary otherwise attends all Board meetings, records all votes and minutes, gives required notices, and may execute authorized conveyances, contracts, or other obligations with the President in the name of the Association.

The full text of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws is presented here in redline, so member districts can see the 2025 proposed amendments within the complete governing document ahead of their vote. A header records the adoption and amendment history: adopted by the Board of Directors on November 15, 2017; adopted by the general membership on January 24, 2018 and October 18, 2018; and amended by member school districts on September 16, 2020, September 10, 2021, and March 3, 2023.

Article I (Offices) locates the Association's principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, and provides for a continuously maintained registered office and registered agent. Article II (Purpose) sets out eight purposes, including advancing the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education, promoting high standards in educational programs and services, making educational-issue information available to board members, conducting meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools, promoting public understanding of the role of school boards, enhancing cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards, presenting a strong unified voice to the area's political representatives, and advocating for county, state, and national legislation supporting public education.

Article III (Membership) provides that any publicly elected Oakland County school district board member, or any elected Oakland ISD board member (collectively 'Member School Districts'), who is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible member. Each member has one vote, exercised in person, with the exception that each member school district has one vote on resolutions (Article IX) and to amend the bylaws (Article XVI); such votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees and must be received before the stated deadline, with results provided to all member districts no later than the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting rights are granted to the Board of Directors only to conduct emergency business and must be reaffirmed at the Board's next meeting; membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV (Dues) provides that the Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District membership dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts. Article V (Meeting of Members) requires an annual meeting - the first regular meeting after July 1 - plus not fewer than three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business; special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Board members with 30 days' notice. Section 3 (Place of Meeting) carries the grammatical correction of 'off' to 'office.' The extracted text continues into the later articles as a marked-up reference copy, showing each amendment in the context of the surrounding provisions.

This marked-up document presents the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions (last revised March 2023) with the 2025 recommended amendments shown, so member districts can review the substance before voting. It notes that resolutions previously adopted by member districts carry their adoption and amendment dates, and cites OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors.

The 2025 recommended amendments to previously adopted resolutions include the following.

Accountability and Transparency (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019): supports transparency and accountability for all school aid funds - community-governed public districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges, and public universities - holding every publicly funded school to the same standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, and naming local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities (referencing MASB Resolution A 6.65). The rationale notes it was expanded to include FOIA, OMA, and additional school entities.

Broadband Access and Devices (OCSBA adopted 9/11/2021): states broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; supports additional federal and state funding to expand affordable, reliable broadband; supports programs to purchase internet-capable devices and software; and adds support for dedicated cybersecurity resources (MASB Resolution A-10.30). Rationale: update 'we support' to 'OCSBA supports' throughout, and add dedicated cybersecurity funding.

Mental Health (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019): supports increased mental-health services and professionals in schools with, at minimum, annual inflation-adjusted state resources, helping staff identify potential mental-health issues and encouraging the Michigan Department of Education to develop a model policy (MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50).

School Aid (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019): opposes using School Aid Fund dollars for any purpose other than K-12 education; specifies the fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and opposes private-school vouchers or tax-credit programs; supports additional funding for special education, at-risk, and ELL students; protects the fund and local revenues from state tax-policy changes; and supports enacting the annual School Aid budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet their June 30 budget requirement (referencing MASB Resolutions A 10.25, A 10.05, A 10.55). The rationale consolidates previously duplicative provisions.

School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021 and 3/3/2023): supports implementation of the SFRC's recommendations, including now-completed studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, while higher-funded districts are held harmless (MASB Resolutions G 11.01, A-10.25).

School Nutrition (OCSBA adopted 3/3/2023): supports expanding the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic codification of free universal meals.

Teacher Shortages (OCSBA adopted 9/11/2021): supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, such as incentives to enter and complete a teaching program, incentives to remain in the classroom, and easing Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states (MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority). A rationale recurring across resolutions is replacing 'we' with 'OCSBA' for consistency.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation titled 'Troy School District, K-5 Writing Curriculum Review,' dated May 6, 2025 and delivered at that evening's Board of Education Workshop. It documents the district's process for reviewing and recommending a new elementary writing curriculum.

The presentation frames the work within the Michigan Department of Education Standards for K-5 Writing, quoting the standards' emphasis on writing to offer and support opinions, demonstrate subject understanding, convey experiences, communicate clearly to external audiences, build knowledge through research, and respond analytically to sources.

The review was carried out by a large Literacy Leadership Team comprising 12 kindergarten teachers, 11 first-grade teachers, 12 second-grade teachers, 11 third-grade teachers, 11 fourth-grade teachers, and 12 fifth-grade teachers, along with 8 special education representatives, 7 literacy specialists, 6 ELD specialists, 3 media specialists, 12 elementary principals, and 8 Teaching & Learning members.

The process began by taking stock of the current state: studying student writing samples from across grade levels and years, reflecting on strengths and growth areas, and reviewing academic, demographic, process, and perception data. Formative assessment drew on Writing Pathways (April 2025), writing rubrics, and a parent survey. The team referenced John Hattie (2023) on high expectations and teacher collaboration, and studied research including 'Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers' (What Works Clearinghouse, IES), Steve Graham's 'Creating a Classroom Vision for Teaching Writing,' the National Writing Project's 'Writing for Life: The Evidence Base for Powerful Writing Instruction,' 'Why Writing Workshops Work: Instilling a Sense of Community and Confidence in Young Writers,' and a review from Zaner-Bloser.

Key findings identified areas of success, including explicit and responsive instruction, student voice and choice, reflections of identity, critical thinking, volume and scope of writing, coverage of state writing standards, and real-world connections and application. Areas of growth included explicit teaching in grammar and spelling, support for handwriting and typing, interdepartmental learning with special education and ELD, and family engagement around writing instruction and support at home.

Communication and engagement efforts included a family survey, principals sharing the review process at PTO meetings to gather feedback, an open family night to review the writing curriculum, and staff engagement through K-5 job-embedded professional learning where teachers were informed and could share feedback.

The recommendation is to adopt Writing Units-of-Study (2024, 2025). Next steps include professional learning in both summer and back-to-school sessions, ongoing job-embedded learning to ensure rigor in writing instruction for all students, continued development of student digital writing portfolios, and parent engagement through celebrations, family letters, and community learning nights.

A consent-agenda item (5.F) on the Troy Board of Education's May 20, 2025 regular meeting agenda, this resolution provides for the statutory public hearing on the district's proposed 2025-2026 school year budget. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses recite the governing Michigan law: every local unit of government, including a school district, must hold a public hearing on its proposed budget, with notice given at least six days before the hearing; the notice must include the time and place of the hearing and state where a copy of the proposed budget is available for public inspection; and the notice must include, in 11-point bold-face type, the statement: THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING. Each local unit must hold the hearing prior to final adoption of its budget.

The operative resolution sets the public hearing for June 17, 2025 at a special Board meeting beginning at 7:00 p.m. at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, for the purpose of receiving testimony and discussing the proposed 2025-2026 budget. It authorizes and directs the Secretary of the Board of Education to publish notice of the hearing, substantially in the form of the attached Exhibit A, in a newspaper of general circulation within the district, at least six days before the hearing and in compliance with all applicable statutory requirements. The document includes blank Yes/No tally lines and a signature block for the Board Secretary, with the statement Resolution declared adopted.

What it is: A background memo supporting the International Academy budget resolutions (agenda 5.G) for the May 20, 2025 meeting. It compares the recommended Amendment 1 revision of the 2024-25 budget against the original budget adopted in June 2024 and presents the proposed 2025-26 budget, with statements by function and by object.

Timing and process:
- Final 2023-24 and original 2024-25 budgets were prepared in mid-March 2024 and approved by the Bloomfield BOE on March 21, 2024. The cooperative agreement requires budgets to the LEAs by March 31 and board approval by end of June, which staff describe as problematic because later adjustments could not be amended.

2024-25 amendment highlights:
- State foundation allowance unchanged at $9,608 per pupil; a new state retirement revenue section rebates about 5.75% of retirement wages for one year.
- Foundation revenue decrease of $271,000; the 147a4 impact is about $223,000 ($123,000 from Bloomfield state aid, $100,000 credited to the IA from districts with staff assigned).
- Combined 2024-25 impact to the IA: a loss of about $48,000. October count-day enrollment: 581 students.
- Recognizes $67,000 of deferred book deposits, with about $20,000 available for 2025-26.
- A social worker's costs, tied to an Oakland County mental health federal grant, are realigned; 31aa mental health state funds offset the 2024-25 costs, with no grant funds available for 2025-26.

2025-26 budget highlights:
- Assumes a $392 per-pupil increase and the full 10% equity cushion; projected enrollment 577 students.
- Reflects attrition savings from two known retirements and elimination of one support position; several districts, including Bloomfield, are in teacher-contract negotiations that may raise the budget.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A background memo from the International Academy's fiscal staff supporting agenda item 5.G at the Troy Board's May 20, 2025 meeting. It accompanies a Revenues by Source and Expenditures by Function document that compares the recommended Amendment 1 revision against the original budget adopted in June 2024, along with a statement by object showing costs by type of activity and the proposed budget for 2025-26. The memo explains that adopted budgets rest on assumptions, primarily pupil enrollment and staffing, and are adjusted as funding, pupil count, and staffing needs become known.

On timing and process, the memo notes that the final 2023-24 and original 2024-25 budgets were prepared in mid-March 2024 with then-known information and were approved by the Bloomfield BOE at the March 21, 2024 meeting. The cooperative agreement requires budgets to be provided to the LEAs by March 31 and approved by their boards of education by the end of June; staff call this timing problematic and prohibitive because adjustments identified later could not be amended under the existing language.

Key 2024-25 assumptions and adjustments: The tuition rate to districts follows the State's target foundation allowance. The original 2024-25 budget assumed a per-pupil increase and flat enrollment, but under the 2024-25 State Aid Budget the foundation allowance remained unchanged at $9,608 per pupil. A new retirement revenue section effectively reduces the retirement rate districts incur for 2024-25; districts still budget the full retirement cost but receive a one-year rebate equal to about 5.75% of retirement wages. The 2024-25 budget is amended to reflect a foundation revenue decrease of $271,000. The impact of the 147a4 provision is roughly $223,000 ($123,000 from Bloomfield state aid revenue and $100,000 as a credit to the IA from districts with staff assigned to the IA), for a combined 2024-25 loss to the IA of about $48,000. Enrollment as of the October count day, used for billing, was 581 students. The 2024-25 budget also recognizes $67,000 of deferred book deposits to offset textbook costs, with about $20,000 available for that purpose in 2025-26, explaining a decrease in local revenue.

The memo describes a correction involving a social worker hired at the IA who was identified as funded by an Oakland County mental health federal grant recorded in Bloomfield's general fund. To align revenue and expenditure sources, the social worker's costs were moved to Bloomfield's general fund; after further investigation, 2022-23 costs were also found recorded in the IA fund with offsetting revenue in Bloomfield's general fund. To correct this, current 31aa mental health state funds will offset the social worker's 2024-25 costs, keeping the expense and revenue in the IA fund. No grant funds are available to continue funding the position in 2025-26 and beyond.

For 2025-26, the budget assumes a $392 per-pupil increase, consistent with the Governor's budget proposal, and applies the full 10% equity cushion. Enrollment is projected from current spring cohorts and known ninth-grade enrollments, counting only ninth graders who passed the entrance exam, yielding a projected 577 students. The 2024-25 expenditure budgets are amended to reflect current needs, including salaries and benefits adjusted to negotiated contracts that vary by district. The 2025-26 expenditure budget was built with precision, incorporating each staff member's 2025-26 salary and retirement plan contribution percentage, attrition savings from two known retirements, and the elimination of one support position. Staff note that several districts, including Bloomfield, are in contract negotiations with their teacher unions and that settled contracts are expected to increase the proposed budget.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A template "ISD Budget Resolution" titled "Support for General Fund Budget" is provided for a constituent local district board of education - here the Troy School District - to formally express support for its intermediate school district's proposed General Fund budget. The resolution contains numerous blanks to be completed with the district name, the type of meeting, the meeting location, the day and time, the board president's name, and the members present and absent, as well as the names of the members offering and supporting the resolution. The preamble sets out two "WHEREAS" clauses citing the Revised School Code: first, that Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended, requires the intermediate school board to submit its proposed General Fund budget no later than May 1 of each year to the board of each constituent district for review; and second, that not later than June 1 of each year the board of each constituent district shall review the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget, shall adopt a board resolution expressing its support for or disapproval of the proposed budget, and shall submit to the intermediate school board any specific objections and proposed changes it has. The operative "Now, therefore be it resolved" section states three things: (1) the board of education has received and reviewed the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget in accordance with Section 624 and, by adopting the resolution, expresses its support for the proposed budget; (2) the secretary of the board of education or a designee shall forward a copy of the resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1; and (3) all resolutions in conflict are rescinded. The document provides lines for recording Ayes and Nays and a statement that the resolution is declared adopted. It closes with a certification block in which the undersigned qualified and acting Secretary of the Board of Education certifies that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted at the meeting, that the original is part of the board's minutes, and that notice of the meeting was given to the public under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended. This is the "support" version of the resolution; a separate "disapproval" version is referenced in the accompanying budget packet.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: The Oakland Schools Original Budget for fiscal year 2025-26 is the proposed budget of the Oakland County intermediate school district (ISD), distributed to constituent districts such as the Troy School District for their review and support/disapproval resolutions. An enterprise-wide overview explains that Oakland Schools is one of 56 Intermediate School Districts established in Michigan in 1962, functioning as a regional service agency providing support services best delivered regionally; it is an autonomous, tax-supported public school district governed by Michigan General School Law. The document sets out the organization's mission ("Every Student. Every Day."), a list of beliefs, a credo, and three organizational objectives: increasing student achievement, serving the diverse needs of schools, and decreasing costs and increasing efficiencies. Under "How We Are Funded," proposed total funding for fiscal year 2025-26 is $503.6 million, composed of property taxes of $259.9 million; other local revenue and investment revenue of $48.0 million; state source revenue of $24.7 million; other financing sources and indirect revenue of $14.0 million; and estimated grant award funding of $157.0 million (funding presented net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund revenues). Under "How We Use Our Resources," proposed total expenditures are $509.7 million, composed of salary, wage, and benefits of $87.1 million; purchased services, supplies, utilities and dues/fees of $25.6 million; capital outlay of $17.8 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds of $218.8 million; grant related expenditures of $157.0 million; and payment on existing debt of $3.4 million. Regarding what is new or of special significance, the budget notes property tax revenue is budgeted to increase by 3.7%, or $9.3 million; taxable values have been increasing incrementally over the last twelve years and finally reached pre-recession levels in 2022-23; and while Oakland County taxable values are expected to increase just over 4.0%, the District uses a conservative estimate until actual taxable values are available. It notes tax abatements leveled off after peaking in fiscal years 2012 and 2013, but an increase in tax tribunal challenges occurred in 2023-24, which the District monitors with the assistance of Oakland County Equalization while holding reserves for anticipated abatement losses. Finally, the budget describes significant projects to renovate and refresh the district's four technical campuses (Oakland Schools Technical Campus, OSTC): Phase I completed an upgrade to the secured entrances for all four OSTC buildings, improving safety and security infrastructure and enhancing the student and guest experience, and included Welcome Centers. The document is dated 04.01.2025.

It separates four clerical/grammatical corrections (typo fixes in Articles V, VIII, IX, and XIV) from three substantive revisions: deleting outdated U.S. mail and fax notice language, adding a new Board Operating Procedures section, and allowing the Secretary role to be split into a Corresponding Secretary and a Recording Secretary.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: "Amendments at a Glance" - a plain-language crosswalk of proposed changes to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, distinguishing non-substantive fixes from content changes.

Four clerical / grammatical revisions (no change in meaning):
1. Art. V, Sec. 3 (Place of Meeting) - correct "off" to "office."
2. Art. VIII, Sec. 2 (Term of Office) - delete stray "r" so "Ther" reads "The."
3. Art. IX, Sec. 4 (Government Relations Committee) - add "on" after "information"; committee remains a standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year.
4. Art. XIV, Sec. 2 (Dealing with the Association) - remove a duplicated phrase.

Three content revisions:
1. Art. VII, Sec. 4 (Notice) - delete outdated language permitting meeting notice by U.S. mail and fax; retain personal, phone, and email notice (at least two days) and mailed notice (five days).
2. Art. VII, Sec. 10 (Board Operating Procedures) - new section requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures used alongside the bylaws (reflecting procedures the Board recently adopted).
3. Art. VIII, Sec. 6 (The Secretary) - permit the Board, annually and at its discretion, to divide the Secretary role into a Corresponding Secretary and a Recording Secretary.

Purpose: Give OCSBA member boards a quick reference before voting on the bylaw amendments.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A summary document titled "OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance," prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) to help its member school district boards - Troy among them - understand a slate of proposed bylaw amendments before voting. It is included in Troy's May 20, 2025 regular meeting packet alongside the full marked-up bylaws. The summary explicitly sorts the proposed changes into those that are merely clerical and those that alter content.

The four clerical/grammatical revisions, stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, are: (1) Article V, Section 3 (Place of Meeting), on page 3, correcting the truncated word "off" to "office"; (2) Article VIII, Section 2 (Term of Office), on page 6, deleting a stray leading "r" so that "Ther" becomes "The"; (3) Article IX, Section 4 (The Government Relations Committee), on page 9, adding the word "on" after "information," with the section confirming the committee is a standing committee whose purpose is to receive information on legislative matters to share with member districts and that it will meet at least six times per year; and (4) Article XIV, Section 2 (Dealing with the Association), on page 15, removing a duplicated phrase in the conflict-of-interest provision governing contracts or transactions between the Association and its directors or officers.

The three substantive content revisions are: (1) Article VII, Section 4 (Notice), on page 5, deleting language that refers to sending meeting notices via U.S. mail and fax as outdated modes of communication, while retaining written notice delivered personally, by phone, or by email at least two days before a special meeting (or five days' notice by mail), plus the standard waiver-of-notice provisions; (2) Article VII, Section 10 (Board Operating Procedures), on page 6, adding a new section directing the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used in conjunction with the bylaws - added because the Board recently adopted such procedures defining roles, responsibilities, and timelines; and (3) Article VIII, Section 6 (The Secretary), on page 7, adding authority for the Board of Directors, on an annual basis and at its discretion, to divide the Office of Secretary into two roles, Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary, which the rationale notes is helpful for a board of seven to nine directors and provides additional leadership opportunity. Each item lists a page number, article, section, and a short rationale.

What it is: Complete bylaws text of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) shown with proposed changes; the redlined companion to the "Amendments at a Glance" summary.

Adoption/amendment history: Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; amendments approved by member school districts 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021, and 3/3/2023.

Article I - Offices: Principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County, Michigan; a registered office/agent is maintained.
Article II - Purpose: Eight aims (a-h), including advancing public education quality in Oakland County through cooperation of locally elected boards, promoting high standards, sharing information with board members, partnering with Oakland Schools, and advocating for county, state, and national legislation supporting public education.
Article III - Membership: Any publicly elected Oakland County board-of-education member, or elected Oakland ISD board member, who is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible member. One vote per member; district votes on resolutions or bylaw amendments are cast one per Member School District. Electronic voting is limited to Board of Directors emergency business, reaffirmed at the next meeting. Membership is not transferable.
Article IV - Dues: Financed by an annual MASB grant to CASBA members, ISD membership dues (not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant), and contributions/gifts.
Article V - Meeting of Members: An annual meeting plus at least three additional regular meetings yearly; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The full text of the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), presented "showing changes" so that member boards - including the Troy School District Board of Education - can review the proposed 2025 amendments in their complete context. The header records the governance history: adopted by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017; adopted by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; and amendments approved by member school districts on 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021, and 3/3/2023.

Article I (Offices) locates the Association's principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan, and provides that it will continuously maintain a registered office and registered agent, with addresses changeable by the Board of Directors.

Article II (Purpose) lists eight purposes, labeled (a) through (h): to advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of locally elected boards; to promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; to make educational-issue information available to school board members; to conduct and sponsor meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; to promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; to enhance cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards; to present a strong voice for Oakland County school boards to political representatives; and to advocate for county, state, and national legislation and governance supporting public education by locally elected boards.

Article III (Membership) provides that the Association is organized on a membership basis: any publicly elected board-of-education member of an Oakland County school district, or any elected Oakland ISD board member (collectively "Member School Districts"), who is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible member. Section 2 grants each Member one vote per matter, all voting done in person, with exceptions: each Member School District has one vote on resolutions (Article IX) or to amend the bylaws (Article XVI), recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees, due before the stated deadline, with results reported to all member districts by the next general membership meeting. Section 3 limits electronic voting to Board of Directors emergency business, to be reaffirmed at the next Board meeting. Section 4 states membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV (Dues) provides the Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, by ISD membership dues in an amount not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts.

Article V (Meeting of Members) requires an annual meeting plus not fewer than three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1, with date, time, and place set by the Board of Directors, and includes provisions for special meetings and place of meeting. The extracted text runs through Article V.

- Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021) - broadband in any infrastructure plan; support for affordable/reliable access, internet-capable devices, and dedicated cybersecurity resources. [MASB A-10.30]

- School Aid (adopted 9/24/2019) - oppose diverting School Aid Fund from K-12; oppose private-school vouchers/tax credits; support Special Ed, At-Risk, and ELL funding; enact the School Aid budget by June 1. [MASB A 10.25, A 10.05, A 10.55]
- School Finance Research Collaborative / SFRC (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023) - support full implementation; higher-funded districts held harmless.
- School Nutrition (adopted 3/3/2023) - expand Free and Reduced Meals to all children.
- Teacher Shortages (adopted 9/11/2021) - support statewide initiatives to recruit and retain teachers.
A recurring edit replaces "We support" with "OCSBA supports" for consistency.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A "showing changes" version of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) advocacy resolutions, listing the 2025 recommended amendments to previously adopted resolutions; the base document is marked "Revised March, 2023." An introductory note states that the resolutions have been adopted by OCSBA's member school districts, that adoption/amendment dates are noted for each, and that - per OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 - resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the Association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. Troy School District, as a member district, reviews the amendments for its vote.

Accountability and Transparency (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019): expanded to support transparency and accountability for ALL school-aid funds - community-governed public districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges, and public universities - holding every publicly funded school to the same standards, expressly including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, and reaching local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Cross-reference MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021): broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding to expand affordable, reliable broadband access, programs to purchase internet-capable devices and software, and dedicated resources for cybersecurity. Cross-reference MASB A-10.30 (2021 amendment). Rationale notes a global change from "we support" to "OCSBA supports" and new cybersecurity funding.

Mental Health (adopted 9/24/2019): OCSBA supports increased mental-health services and professionals in schools with at least annual inflation-adjusted state resources, helping staff identify potential student mental-health issues and encouraging the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) to develop a model policy for staff response. Cross-references MASB G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50.

School Aid (adopted 9/24/2019): oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for anything but K-12; specify in Michigan's Constitution that the Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th-grade public education and oppose private-school vouchers or tax-credit programs; support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and ELL students; protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax-policy changes; and enact the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can adopt budgets by June 30. Cross-references MASB A 10.25 (a), (c), (g), (h), (j); A 10.05; A 10.55. Rationale notes deduplication of overlapping bullets.

School Finance Research Collaborative / SFRC (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023): OCSBA supports implementation of the SFRC recommendations, including the completed additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, while higher-funded districts must be held harmless. Cross-references MASB G 11.01 and A-10.25.

School Nutrition (adopted 3/3/2023): supports expanding the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as done during the pandemic-era universal free meals. Teacher Shortages (adopted 9/11/2021): OCSBA supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality preparation programs - incentives to enter and complete teaching programs, incentives to remain in the classroom, and easing Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states. Cross-reference MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

The letter projects 3.7% growth in Oakland Schools' property-tax revenue, a 2.0% salary increase plus step increases, roughly $1.4 million in software/instructional subsidies, and a PA-18 Special Education base-distribution increase of about $10.3 million (5.9%).

A signed transmittal letter dated April 1, 2025, from Kenneth Gutman, Superintendent of Oakland Schools (the Oakland ISD), inviting the boards of education of its constituent districts - Troy School District among them - to review the proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2025-26. It is included in Troy's May 20, 2025 board packet because, under the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2025-26 General Fund budget must be submitted to constituent district boards for review, and each constituent board must, not later than June 1, adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency Oakland Schools includes budgets for all of its funds, but constituent districts vote only on the General Fund.

On revenue, the letter notes Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property taxes and projects a growth factor of 3.7% in its property-tax revenues, describing this as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable-value increase projections. On personnel, the budget includes step increases for eligible employees plus a 2.0% salary increase for all staff, with all union salary changes and step adjustments subject to collective bargaining. Oakland Schools provides almost $1.4 million in subsidies for software and other instructional tools in Career and Technical Education and in curriculum and assessment, exclusive of pass-through grants, other district allocations, and dedicated support staff.

On PA-18 Special Education funding (property-tax revenue Oakland Schools receives to support special education), the base distribution to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $10.3 million, or 5.9%. An additional $2.5 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group-home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special-education program startup, extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2024-25 Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.6 million above the base distribution.

The Enterprise-Wide Executive Summary is cited for key projects and initiatives in the 2025-26 budget, listed as: Oakland Schools Technical Campus Renovations; Artificial Intelligence; Social-Emotional Wellbeing and Mental Health Support; Business Office Residency Program; HR Leadership Academy; Essential Practices in Instruction - Capacity & Coherence (EPIC) Numeracy Project; Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO); Nanotechnology, Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology (NAIS) Lab; and Shared Services. Oakland Schools states it uses a five-year forecast (updated with each budget amendment, incorporating Oakland County Equalization taxable-value projections) and a five-year capital plan updated annually.

The letter lays out the process and timeline: the proposed General Fund budget is to be submitted to constituent boards by May 1; a presentation to the district business managers is scheduled at the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 11, 2025; the Oakland Schools Board of Education will hold a Designates Meeting on April 23 at 6:00 PM for local board designates and administration to review the General Fund budget before submitting their board's resolution on or before June 1, 2025; and the Board will hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 3 and consider the FY 2025-26 proposed budget for approval that night. Questions are directed to Gutman's office at 248.209.2424; copies go to the district superintendent and district business manager.

A cost estimate from First Student, the Troy School District's pupil transportation contractor, presenting route counts, per-route daily rates, and projected annual costs across three school years: 2024-2025, 2025-2026, and 2026-2027. The estimate accompanies the proposed renewal and pricing update of the district's transportation services contract.

Route counts and daily rates (2024-25, 2025-26, 2026-27) are: Regular Education Daily, 32 routes at $282.90, $306.78, and $334.39; Special Education in District, 17 routes at $338.28, $454.93, and $495.87; Special Education out of District, 7 routes at $338.28, $454.93, and $495.87; Extra-Curricular/Field Trips at $65.34, $69.91, and $76.20; Mid-Day/Shuttles, 24 at $62.57, $78.33, and $85.38; 8 Monitors (64 hours per day) at $31.43, $33.63, and $36.66 per hour; Special Education Summer, 20 routes at $338.28, $379.63, and $413.80; and Regular Education Summer, 2 routes at $282.90, $306.78, and $334.39.

Annual costs are computed over 175 school days for daily service and 60 days for summer service. By category for 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27: Regular Education Daily $1,584,240.00, $1,717,968.00, $1,872,585.12; Special Education in District $1,006,383.00, $1,353,416.75, $1,475,224.26; Special Education out of District $414,393.00, $557,289.25, $607,445.28; Mid-Day/Shuttles $262,794.00, $328,986.00, $358,594.74; 8 Monitors $352,016.00, $376,656.00, $410,555.04; Special Education Summer $405,936.00, $455,556.00, $496,556.04; and Regular Education Summer $33,948.00, $36,813.60, $40,126.82. Extra-Curricular/Field Trips are shown at zero annual cost (no guaranteed days).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A legislative overview presentation on Michigan's Public Act 146 of 2024, the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law, prepared by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D. (mimtsstac.org) and dated June 2025. It explains that PA 146 and companion PA 147, signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, revise the Read by Grade Three statute (1280f), extend Individual Reading Improvement Plans across grades K-3, and set literacy screening requirements for K-3 and grades 4-12. The overview defines dyslexia, lists its characteristics, and details a code-emphasis, MTSS-based (Tier 1-3) approach to reading instruction and intervention.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Informational overview presented to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop of June 3, 2025, authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D. (Michigan MTSS Technical Assistance Center, mimtsstac.org), dated June 2025.
- Subject: Public Act 146 of 2024, the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law.

The law
- Bipartisan Public Acts 146 and 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, to improve reading outcomes for K-12 learners and affect in-service and pre-service teachers; the law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.
- PA 146 revises the Read by Grade Three statute (1280f): Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span K-3; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; district-identified coaches are added; de-identified IRIP data is reported to ISDs, aggregated, and sent to MDE.

Assessment requirements
- K-3: reliable, valid screening and progress-monitoring for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense-word reading, rapid automized naming (RAN), oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension.
- Grades 4-12: students showing indicators (avoidance, effortful reading, comprehension/decoding difficulty, spelling/encoding difficulty, low ELA/literacy performance, reading deficiency) are screened from MDE's approved list; those needing Tier 2 support are screened at least three times per year.

Dyslexia and instruction
- Provides the statutory dyslexia definition (a neurobiological specific learning disorder) and K-3 and 4-12 characteristics from the MDE Dyslexia Handbook.
- Outlines MTSS Tier 1 class-wide instruction using a code-emphasis instructional approach and Tiers 2-3 intensified intervention, documented in the IRIP.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Legislative overview presentation titled PA 146 Legislative Overview, authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., of the Michigan Multi-Tiered System of Supports Technical Assistance Center (mimtsstac.org) and dated June 2025. It was included in the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop materials for June 3, 2025 to brief the Board on Michigan's new K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law.

The law: Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, with the goal of improving reading outcomes for K-12 learners and impacting both in-service and pre-service teachers. Frequently referred to as the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law, PA 146 is expressly not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia. PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. Among the 1280f changes: Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span grades K-3 (development of 4th-grade IRIPs is not included in PA 146, though MDE is examining K-12 language to clarify requirements beyond 3rd grade); a level of IRIP information must be reported to ISDs with de-identified student information, then aggregated and sent to MDE; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; and the term district-identified coaches is infused into the language.

Assessment requirements, K-3: Reliable and valid screening and progress-monitoring measures are required for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense-word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension (retelling, cloze reading procedure). A Rapid Automized Naming (RAN) measure, used to identify dyslexia characteristics, gauges cognitive processing speed by having students name known colors, objects, letters, or words under timed conditions; teachers should not be asked to teach students how to improve their RAN data.

Assessment requirements, grades 4-12: Only adolescents demonstrating certain indicators need a screening assessment to confirm dyslexia consequences. Indicators include escape or avoidance behaviors around reading or writing, effortful or laborious reading, reading comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading, significant spelling or encoding difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties, low performance on approved English language arts standards, low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments, and reading deficiency. Students showing these indicators must be screened using a reliable and valid assessment from MDE's approved list; where data confirm the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, students will need access to intervention and be screened at least three times per year.

Dyslexia definition and characteristics: PA 146 defines dyslexia as a specific learning disorder that is neurobiological in origin, characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities that typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language, often unexpected relative to other cognitive abilities and effective instruction, and that may include secondary consequences such as reading-comprehension problems and reduced reading experience. Sample characteristics drawn from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook (p. 15) are listed separately for K-3 and for grades 4-12.

Instruction and MTSS: The law outlines Tier 1 class-wide reading instruction, including new language on curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a code-emphasis instructional approach (direct, explicit instruction on written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level to build automaticity), while Tiers 2 and 3 outline methods to intensify literacy intervention; K-3 intervention must be documented in the IRIP.
