https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
PowerPoint presentation (13 slides) titled PA 146 Legislative Overview, authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., of the Michigan MTSS Technical Assistance Center (mimtsstac.org), dated June 2025. It is the slide-deck counterpart to the PA 146 PDF included in the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop materials for June 3, 2025, and its content mirrors that overview.

The law (slides 1-4): Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, with the goal of improving reading outcomes for K-12 learners and impacting in-service and pre-service teachers. Commonly called the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law, PA 146 is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia. PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute: Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span K-3 (4th-grade IRIPs are not included, though MDE is examining K-12 clarifications); IRIP information at a de-identified level must be reported to ISDs, aggregated, and sent to MDE; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; and district-identified coaches are added to the language.

Assessment requirements (slides 5-8): For K-3, reliable and valid screening and progress-monitoring measures are required for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense-word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension (retelling, cloze reading procedure). Rapid Automized Naming (RAN) is used to identify dyslexia characteristics by measuring cognitive processing speed through timed naming of known colors, objects, letters, or words; teachers should not be asked to teach students to improve RAN data. For grades 4-12, only adolescents demonstrating indicators need a confirming screening assessment; indicators include escape or avoidance behaviors around reading or writing, effortful or laborious reading, comprehension difficulties from inaccurate or inefficient word reading, significant spelling or encoding difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties, low performance on approved ELA standards, low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments, and reading deficiency. Students showing indicators are screened using a reliable, valid assessment from MDE's approved list; those confirmed as needing Tier 2 reading intervention receive intervention and are screened at least three times per year.

Dyslexia definition and characteristics (slides 9-12): The deck presents the statutory definition of dyslexia as a neurobiological specific learning disorder characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities, typically resulting from a deficit in the phonological component of language, often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and effective instruction, and potentially carrying secondary consequences such as reading-comprehension problems and reduced reading experience. Sample characteristics from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook (p. 15) are provided for K-3 (for example, confusing letters with similar sounds, repeatedly misspelling taught letter-sound combinations, difficulty with handwriting, avoiding reading activities, and word-finding difficulty when speaking) and for grades 4-12 (difficulty reading and spelling multisyllabic words, difficulty understanding new text due to decoding and word-recognition issues, limited vocabulary, weaker written expression than peers, and avoidance of reading and writing).

Instruction and MTSS (slide 13): The law outlines Tier 1 class-wide reading instruction with new language on curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a code-emphasis instructional approach, while Tiers 2 and 3 outline how to intensify literacy intervention; K-3 students needing support must have it documented in the Individual Reading Improvement Plan (the term Individual Reading Intervention Plan also appears, pending MDE clarification).

What it is:

- Provides that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law.

Who:
Certified by Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education. The Moved/Supported and Yes/No adoption lines are blank in this draft.

Establish district policy encouraging safe firearm storage and expand gun-violence-prevention outreach to Troy families.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented as agenda item 3.D under the Recognition portion of the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting held June 17, 2025, this is a suggested Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage placed before the Board for acceptance. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution; the Moved by, Supported by, and Yes/No vote lines remain blank in this draft copy.

The resolution opens with a series of whereas clauses establishing its rationale. It states that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District, and that firearm-related death is the leading cause of death among children and adolescents. It cites that death rates from firearms among youth ages 14 to 17 are now 22.5% higher than motor-vehicle-related death rates, making middle- and high-school-age children more likely to die from a firearm injury than from any other single cause. Drawing on a U.S. Secret Service report, it notes that in incidents of gun violence on school grounds, 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative. Additional clauses state that roughly 350 children under age 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or someone else each year, that nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide annually including over 950 children and teens, and that research indicates 47% of firearm owners with children living in their homes do not safely store at least one weapon. The resolution asserts that secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe and that protecting students, teachers, and staff from gun violence is the responsibility of all adult stakeholders.

The operative provisions follow. The Board directs the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm-safety and violence-prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing secure storage of firearms by including it in the district's annual notification materials. It further resolves that the Board and Superintendent will continue to work with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to collaborate and increase efforts to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure firearm storage and other gun-violence-prevention safety measures. A final clause provides that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law.

The document closes with a certification by Emina Alic, Secretary of the Board of Education, attesting that the resolution was duly adopted at the regular meeting held June 17, 2025, in compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976). Source citations appended to the resolution include University of Michigan news and health-lab reports on firearm deaths among children, the U.S. Secret Service publication Protecting America's Schools, Everytown Research materials on unintentional shootings and the rise of firearm suicide among young Americans, a Pew Research Center report, and David C. Grossman et al., Gun Storage Practices and Risk of Youth Suicide and Unintentional Firearm Injuries, JAMA 293, no. 6 (2005): 707-14.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Consent agenda item 6.J at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of June 17, 2025, this suggested resolution authorizes a second round of Schools of Choice enrollment under Section 105 for the 2025-2026 school year. The item explains that, in accordance with Michigan state law, school districts must pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. It notes that the first round of Schools of Choice, approved in February 2025, has been closed to applicants, and that the district did not fill all of the seats previously approved; it therefore recommends approving additional seats.

The resolution cites MCL 388.1705 (Section 105), which provides students the option to enroll in another school district within the same intermediate school district as their own. Pursuant to Section 105, the Troy School District will accept additional Schools of Choice applications for students who attend a school district within Oakland County. The additional seats offered are twenty-five (25) at Kindergarten and twenty-five (25) at First Grade.

The recommended action is to adopt the resolution, which states that the Board of Education of the Troy School District, exercising the option permitted by Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept additional applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2025-2026 school year for twenty-five (25) kindergarten and twenty-five (25) first grade nonresident students who attend a school district within Oakland County. The Moved by, Supported by, and Yes/No vote lines are left blank in this draft.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A comprehensive annual budget presentation prepared and delivered by Dan Trudel, CPA, to the Troy School District Board of Education on June 17, 2025. It addresses truth in taxation and the establishment of millage rates, General Fund budget adjustments and assumptions, and budgets for the ancillary, capital projects, debt, sinking, capital maintenance, and special revenue funds, together with the 2024-2025 final amendments and the 2025-2026 budget proposals.

Taxable values rose year over year: 2024 total taxable value was $5,334,440,800 (homestead $3,479,524,110; non-homestead $1,854,916,690), increasing to a 2025 total of $5,614,905,650 (homestead $3,652,141,670; non-homestead $1,962,763,980). The presentation reviews the components of school taxation - the 18-mill operating levy on non-homestead property, the 6-mill State Education Tax on all property toward the foundation allowance, and the sinking fund and debt levies - and explains the Headlee Amendment rollback and Hold Harmless mechanisms. The 2025 millage rates cited are: general operating of 18.0000 mills on all other non-homestead property, 2.5796 mills homestead, and 8.5796 mills commercial personal property; Sinking Fund 0.9540 mills on all property; and Debt Fund 6.1000 mills on all property, with the State Education Tax at 6.0000 mills. Total millage for 2025-2026 is 15.6336 mills (homestead) and 31.0540 mills (non-homestead).

For the General Fund, the 2024-2025 original budget projected revenues of $191,544,523 and expenditures of $195,485,356; Amendment #3 revised these to revenues of $194,857,883 and expenditures of $198,652,719, yielding an ending fund balance of $32,979,691 (16.60%). The proposed 2025-2026 original budget sets revenues at $190,545,984 and expenditures at $194,285,613, a change in fund balance of ($3,739,629) and an ending fund balance of $29,240,062 (15.05%). The 2024-2025 adjustments reflect final categorical, federal grant, and ISD allocations plus updated purchased services, salaries, and benefits. Key 2025-2026 assumptions: use of the lowest proposed foundation allowance and categorical figures among the Governor, House, and Senate budgets; a blended FTE count of 12,100, down from the current 12,274; a lowest proposed foundation allowance increase of $392 per pupil; and a target of $5 million in General Fund expenditure reductions.

Other fund budgets (2025-2026 proposed) include: the 2019 Capital Projects Fund with expenditures of $1,034,912 drawing its balance to $0; the 2023 Capital Projects Fund with revenues of $3,996,374, expenditures of $67,063,907, and an ending balance of $38,932,867 (down from $102,000,400); the Debt Fund with revenues of $31,855,092 and expenditures of $32,070,536; the Sinking Fund with revenues of $5,225,572 and expenditures of $2,125,000 (ending balance $3,177,029); and the Capital Maintenance Fund with revenues of $2,000,000 and expenditures of $700,000 (ending balance $1,772,125). The presentation supports Board adoption of the 2024-2025 final budget amendment and the 2025-2026 original budgets across all funds. (The extracted text is truncated mid-document.)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (dated May 6, 2025) reporting on the district's K-5 writing curriculum review and recommending adoption of the Writing Units of Study (2024, 2025). The review was led by a Literacy Leadership Team of elementary teachers, principals, literacy and ELD specialists, and special education representatives, drawing on student writing samples, formative assessment via Writing Pathways, and parent and staff surveys. Among the reviewed programs, Writing Units of Study was preferred by 90% of reviewers, and all 24 early-adopter teachers reported that the updated units helped their instruction and impacted student learning.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Troy School District presentation, dated May 6, 2025, documenting the K-5 writing curriculum review and recommending adoption of the Writing Units of Study (2024, 2025) curriculum for elementary writing instruction. The review was framed around the Michigan Department of Education's K-5 writing standards, which emphasize writing to offer and support opinions, demonstrate subject understanding, convey experiences, and build knowledge through research.

The work was carried out by a broadly representative Literacy Leadership Team that included 12 kindergarten teachers, 11 first grade teachers, 12 second grade teachers, 11 third grade teachers, 11 fourth grade teachers, and 12 fifth grade teachers, along with 7 literacy specialists, 6 ELD specialists, 3 media specialists, 8 special education representatives, 12 elementary principals, and 8 Teaching & Learning members. The team began by studying student writing samples across grade levels and years and conducting a data review spanning academic, demographic, process, and perception data. Formative assessment used the Writing Pathways tool (April 2025), and the process incorporated a parent survey and reflection on writing rubrics. The presentation cites education researcher John Hattie (2023) on maintaining high expectations for all students and on the value of teacher collaboration.

Key findings identified areas of success - explicit and responsive instruction, student voice and choice, reflections of identity, critical thinking, volume and scope of writing, coverage of state writing standards, and real-world connections - and areas of growth: explicit teaching in grammar and spelling, support for handwriting and typing, interdepartmental learning with special education and ELD, and family engagement around writing instruction. The team drew on external resources including the What Works Clearinghouse (IES) practice guide "Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers," Steve Graham's work on creating a classroom vision for teaching writing, the National Writing Project's "Writing for Life," and a Zaner-Bloser review of writing workshops.

In evaluating curricular options, reviewers expressed a strong preference for Writing Units of Study (90%), followed by Benchmark Education Writing Workshop (6%) and Being a Writer (4%), with Step Up to Writing and Writing By Design each at 0%; the review purposely considered only K-5 programs offering year-long writing curricula. An early-adopter cohort of 24 classroom teachers, representing every grade level and every school, reported that 100% found the updated writing units of study helpful to their instruction and impactful on student learning, and that identified needs - grammar, spelling, tools for ensuring access for all, and family engagement - had been addressed in the updated units.

The recommendation is to adopt Writing Units-of-Study (2024, 2025), supported by professional learning in summer and back-to-school sessions, ongoing job-embedded learning, continued development of student digital writing portfolios, and parent engagement through family letters, celebrations, and community learning nights. Family and staff engagement included principals sharing the review process at PTO meetings, an open family night, and feedback opportunities at K-5 job-embedded professional learning.

What it is
Proposed consent-agenda resolution (agenda item 5.F.) for the Troy School District Board of Education to accept settlement terms in Batista v Office of Retirement Services, a Michigan pension-calculation lawsuit.

Background
- Litigation ongoing since 2019, filed by the Michigan Association of Superintendents and Administrators to challenge the Office of Retirement Services' restrictions on retirement pension benefits (how compensation increases count toward employees' state pensions).
- The parties reached a settlement on May 16, 2025 (Case No. 19-000019-MZ).
- The settlement lets local boards adopt resolutions attesting that compensation was not paid specifically to increase final average compensation ('spiking').

Resolution text
The board certifies it has never provided a compensation increase for the purpose of 'spiking' an employee's final average compensation as calculated by the Office of Retirement Services, and states the resolution is intended to comply with the settlement terms and be interpreted accordingly in any future proceeding between the district's employees and the Office of Retirement Services.

Action
Recommended action is acceptance of the resolution; the motion, support, and Yes/No vote lines are blank in this draft. (The July 15, 2025 board minutes record this item's approval as consent-agenda item F, 6-0.)

Purpose
Satisfies a condition of the Batista settlement so that affected employees' pension calculations are protected.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This item is the proposed board resolution accepting the 'Settlement Terms of Batista v Office of Retirement Services Litigation,' presented as agenda item 5.F. under the consent portion of a Troy School District Board of Education meeting.

Background stated in the document: Litigation over the calculation of Michigan school-district administrator wages has been ongoing since Batista v Office of Retirement Services was initiated in 2019. The Michigan Association of Superintendents and Administrators filed the suit to challenge the Office of Retirement Services' 'arbitrary restrictions' on retirement pension benefits. The parties reached a settlement agreement on May 16, 2025, in Case No. 19-000019-MZ, concluding a longstanding dispute between Michigan public-school employees and the Michigan Office of Retirement Services over what compensation increases may count toward employees' state pensions. Under the settlement, local boards of education have the opportunity to pass resolutions 'attesting that the subject compensation [paid to employees] was not paid for the specific purpose of increasing final average compensation (also known as spiking).'

The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution. The resolution's whereas clauses recite that the Board of Education of Troy School District has historically provided compensation and increases to all employees in consideration of their labor and efforts, and that the May 16, 2025 settlement allows the attestation described above. The operative language provides that the Board of Education certifies it has never provided an increase to any employees' compensation for the purpose of spiking the amount of that employees' final average compensation, as calculated by the Office of Retirement Services. It further states that the resolution is acknowledged by the board to comply with the settlement terms of Batista v Office of Retirement Services and should be interpreted as such in any future proceeding or controversy between the district's employees and the Michigan Office of Retirement Services.

The draft leaves the mover, supporter, and Yes/No vote lines blank; the Troy Board of Education's July 15, 2025 minutes record this settlement item being approved 6-0 as consent-agenda item F.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum from the Troy School District Teaching & Learning department, dated August 8, 2025, recommending the purchase of additional AP Human Geography textbooks. It is addressed to Dan Trudel, CPA, Assistant Superintendent of Business, from David Recker, Ed.D., Director of Teaching & Learning, with a copy to Donna Havrilla. The department is located at 4420 Livernois Rd., Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.5221).

Context and rationale. The district reports that it has increased student access to AP Human Geography at its high schools but was unable to procure enough copies of the 12th-edition textbook currently in use, from either the publisher or the secondary market. In response, the department attached quotes to purchase The Cultural Landscape: An Introduction to Human Geography, 14th Edition. The memo notes the textbook can only be purchased through Pearson and has been reviewed by CIS, department heads, and instructors of the course, and is an approved text by the College Board. The textbook review committee enthusiastically endorsed upgrading from the 12th edition to the 14th edition.

Requested purchase. The department requests 130 units for Troy High School at $24,078.60 and 180 units for Athens High School at $33,339.60, for a grand total of $57,418.20 as an expenditure of the General Fund. This total includes both the physical textbook and six years of online access. A purchase summary is attached as supporting documentation, and the memo invites questions. This recommendation underlies the corresponding consent-agenda resolution approving the $57,418.20 purchase and is supported by two Pearson quotes covering the Troy High School and Athens High School orders respectively.
